material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Catalyst and solvent identities will interact with reaction temperature/time; a useful starting screen is categorical because indices imply no ordering. Prediction: at least one catalyst–solvent combination heated near 350 K for about 20 min will give materially higher conversion/selectivity than the others. A reaction-stage HPLC will be used diagnostically in each batch; final assays remain decisive.

## H2 [tentative]
Within the dossier scope, X2 has the largest nominal product/impurity selectivity (S*≈3.30) and product organic fraction. Prediction: X2 extraction into an organic phase followed by an aqueous-compatible wash will improve final purity, though recovery may require a large organic/aqueous ratio. Because the dossier may be misindexed, this remains a prior, not a conclusion.

## Decision rule
First screen reaction categories while holding workup broadly constant; later batches will repeat or refine the best observed qualifying process. Prefer the completed batch with highest observed recovery among final purity ≥0.80, considering assay uncertainty and repeatability. A nonqualifying purity result overrides a recovery advantage.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [narrowed, tentatively supported]
At 350 K, catalyst identity strongly affects target formation in the tested matched-solvent runs. C2/S2 gave the best reaction-stage HPLC target yield (≈0.090) and selectivity (≈0.57; runner-operation-0036), versus C0/S0 (≈0.031, 0.42; runner-operation-0006), C1/S1 (≈0.065, 0.36; runner-operation-0022), and C3/S3 (≈0.079, 0.37; runner-operation-0050). These are confounded catalyst–solvent pairs, so catalyst superiority is not yet isolated. Prediction: C2 paired with other solvents and higher temperature will retain or improve this advantage.

## H2 [partly supported, scope uncertain]
X2 extraction plus wash produced the only qualifying final purity so far (0.803 in batch 3; runner-operation-0045), but recovery was only 0.036. Other matched reaction feeds did not qualify, so workup performance is confounded by feed composition. The nominal dossier remains directionally plausible but not validated against other extractants.

## H3 [new, unresolved]
Reaction-stage HPLC and final assay conversion disagree sharply (e.g. ≈0.173 before quench versus ≈0.993 final in batch 3). Quench/workup may continue or alter conversion, or the metrics may have different phase/process scopes. Treat final purity/recovery as authoritative for selection and use HPLC only comparatively at its declared stage.

## Decision
Continue with C2 solvent/temperature screening. Keep X2, 0.04 L organic, and 0.04 L wash initially; later test wash intensity or extractant only after a stronger feed is found. Selection remains highest final recovery among purity ≥0.80.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only within tested scope]
C2/S2 at 350 K for 2400 s is the most reliable route to qualifying material among tested categorical conditions. Batch 3 qualified at purity 0.803 and recovery 0.0364 (runner-operation-0045). Nominal repeats with different extractants/workups showed reaction-stage variability (runner-operation-0120, -0134, -0148, -0162), so the magnitude of the advantage is uncertain; nonetheless no other catalyst–solvent family produced a qualifying result with higher recovery.

## H2 [qualified and revised]
X2 is the best observed recovery-oriented extractant at the purity boundary. X0 and X1 gave qualifying purity but lower recovery (batch 9: 0.814/0.0304, runner-operation-0129; batch 10: 0.820/0.0217, runner-operation-0143). X3 did not qualify (0.784, runner-operation-0157). Increasing X2 organic ratio and applying two washes raised batch-12 purity to 0.823 but recovery was only 0.0294 (runner-operation-0172), opposing the expectation that the larger organic volume would improve net recovery after washing. Extra wash loss and batch variability are unresolved alternatives.

## H3 [scope warning]
The persistent disparity between reaction-stage HPLC conversion and final conversion means those values must not be treated as repeated measurements of one material. Final assay recovery and purity are the authoritative selection metrics; carried readings are not evidence of later-stage composition.

## Final decision
Recommend completed batch 3: C2/S2, 350 K, 2400 s; quench; add 0.03 L aqueous and 0.04 L X2; mix 240 s at 700 rpm, settle 300 s, keep organic, wash 0.04 L, terminate and assay. It has the highest observed recovery among batches meeting purity ≥0.80. The purity margin is small relative to assay standard uncertainty (0.008), so confirmation would be prudent in real follow-up; within the completed campaign, batch 3 remains the rule-consistent choice.

payload.rationale: These are extrapolations from the sealed campaign, not new observations. All queries use the untested C1/S2 pairing, only 0.00025 mol catalyst, smaller aqueous volumes, drying, 600 s concentration in most cases, and a 0.97 transfer; therefore the intervals are intentionally much wider than final-assay noise alone. For Q01–Q06, the catalyst/reagent ratio is twenty-fold below the campaign ratio, so I predict very low recovery. Longer heating should raise recovery but accumulate more impurity, making Q02 less pure than Q01. At the common long-time feed, X0 should extract less target but enrich it more strongly than X2 (Q03 versus Q04). A smaller X2 organic phase should likewise favor purity over recovery (Q05 versus Q06); the pre-separation HPLC sample is proportionally most consequential for Q05. For Q07–Q12, reducing reagent to 0.002 mol restores the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio, so appreciably greater fractional recovery is expected despite dilution. Washing should raise purity while losing target (Q07 versus Q08). Two staged 0.01 L washes should be somewhat more discriminating, but slightly more lossy, than one 0.02 L wash (Q09 versus Q10). Concentration is expected mainly to remove solvent; I assign Q12 essentially the same purity as Q11 but modestly lower recovery because additional handling or thermal loss is plausible. The dominant uncertainty is the unidentified response to catalyst loading, dilution, and the C1/S2 interaction, followed by run-to-run variability observed among nominal C2/S2 repeats.

payload.report:
1. Claims and laws

No instance-specific prior mechanism or optimum was supplied. The only substantive prior was the nominal extractant dossier; material indices were explicitly anonymous categories.

Supported, within the tested scope:
• The self-developed claim that reaction conditions create a conversion–selectivity tradeoff. Extending C2/S2 at 350 K from 2400 s in batch 3 to 7200 s in batch 8 increased reaction-stage HPLC yield from 0.0902 to 0.2274 and final recovery from 0.0364 to 0.0542, but final purity fell from 0.8034 to 0.6584. This comparison most clearly changed my judgment from expecting time mainly to improve production to expecting impurity accumulation as well.
• The claim that C2/S2 is favorable under moderate conditions. Batch 3 had reaction-stage selectivity 0.572 and was the highest-recovery qualifying final batch. This is support for the combination, not an independently identified C2 effect.
• The qualitative partition/wash law that purification trades recovery for purity. Batches 9, 10, and 12 achieved higher purity than batch 3 but lower recovery. Batch 12, with two washes, reached purity 0.8233 but recovery only 0.0294.
• The dossier’s qualitative preference for X2 was partly supported. Batch 3 with X2 had higher qualifying recovery than X0 in batch 9 or X1 in batch 10, while X3 in batch 11 failed the purity requirement. The comparisons were confounded by feed variability, so the numerical dossier constants were not validated.

Contradicted or revised:
• The expectation that increasing X2 organic volume would necessarily improve net recovery was contradicted by batch 12. Its larger organic phase plus two washes gave lower recovery than batch 3; phase-ratio benefit, wash loss, and batch variability remain inseparable.
• Any assumption that reaction-stage and final conversion were measurements of the same material was contradicted by their large systematic disparity. For example, batch 3 had HPLC conversion 0.173 before quench but final conversion 0.993. The instrument contract also warned that stages have different scopes.
• A simple “more conversion is better” rule was contradicted by batches 5–8: they had comparatively high reaction-stage production and final recovery, but all failed the purity constraint.

Untested or unidentified:
• Separate catalyst and solvent effects, because the initial screen changed both together.
• Arrhenius parameters, kinetic reaction orders, and whether target loss is chemical degradation or phase/speciation behavior.
• The quantitative equilibrium-partition equation under process conditions.
• Independent effects of drying and concentration; only batch 1 combined them, with a different and weak feed.
• Independent effects of phase ratio and wash staging, since batch 12 changed both.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one C2/S2 batch at 350 K with the campaign loading and collect small HPLC samples at predetermined times, for example 1200, 2400, 4800, and 7200 s, followed by another measurement immediately after quenching but before extraction. The sampling volumes would be fixed in advance and included in the mass balance. The batch would then receive the batch-3 workup and final assay.

This would distinguish the leading kinetic explanation—parallel impurity formation or product degradation during extended heating—from the alternative that reporter/speciation or downstream phase changes create the apparent loss of selectivity.

• If target amount first rose and then fell while byproduct increased continuously during heating, I would strengthen the degradation/sequential-reaction explanation.
• If target and impurity evolved monotonically during heating but changed abruptly only after quench, I would favor quench chemistry or reporter/speciation changes.
• If reactor HPLC remained nearly unchanged while final outcomes still varied greatly, I would shift emphasis toward extraction, phase selection, or measurement-scope effects.
• If all time points reproduced one smooth conversion curve without declining selectivity, I would reject degradation as the main cause and interpret batch 3 versus batch 8 chiefly as run variability or downstream coupling.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

I did not fully exploit the raw spectral traces, peak-shape information, replicate-signal structure, or detailed characterization artifacts. Final degradation-warning channels were mostly small, but they were not sufficient to identify chemical degradation and were not central to selection. Cost and safety data were monitored, but they contributed little to the recovery-with-purity objective because tested batches remained within the safety limit. The dossier’s two anchor compositions were used qualitatively rather than fitted quantitatively. Final-assay yield and selectivity channels were secondary to the explicitly defined purity and recovery metrics.

The sealed recommendation is least reliable with respect to robustness at the purity boundary: batch 3 measured purity 0.8034, only 0.0034 above the requirement and less than the declared 0.008 assay standard uncertainty. Nominal C2/S2 repeats also showed appreciable variation. It remains the correct observed-data choice, but not a demonstrated high-confidence process capability result.

The blind predictions are especially uncertain for Q01–Q06 because their catalyst/reagent ratio is twenty-fold below the campaign ratio and the C1/S2 interaction was never measured. Q07–Q12 are also extrapolations to a twenty-fold smaller reagent charge, strong dilution, drying, transfer, and mostly concentration. The predictions comparing concentration (Q11–Q12) are particularly weak because the campaign did not isolate that operation. Absolute recoveries are less reliable than the directional paired contrasts.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. I prioritized completing all twelve final assays, finding any process above purity 0.80, and then maximizing observed recovery. That encouraged broad screening followed by workup refinement, but discouraged clean replication, serial kinetics, independent phase assays, and a balanced factorial design. There was no clear conflict with the stated goal, but there was an identification-versus-optimization tradeoff: the campaign found an admissible recommendation more effectively than it identified a unique quantitative mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 3 had the highest observed final-assay recovery (0.0364) among completed batches satisfying the purity constraint (purity 0.8034 >= 0.80). It used C2/S2 at 350 K for 2400 s followed by X2 extraction, organic-phase retention, and one 0.04 L wash. Higher-purity alternatives (batches 9, 10, and 12) had lower recovery.
